title: Ser or estar
text: Use estar for temporary states and feelings (Estoy cansado) and for location (Estoy en Madrid). Use ser for identity, origin, profession and permanent characteristics (Soy estudiante, Soy de México).

title: The verb gustar
text: Gustar agrees with the thing that is liked, not with the person: Me gusta el libro, but Me gustan los perros. The person goes in the indirect object pronoun: me, te, le, nos, os, les.

title: The preterite for finished past actions
text: Use the preterite for completed actions at a specific time in the past, often with ayer, anoche or la semana pasada: Ayer comí pizza. The present tense (como) cannot describe yesterday.

title: Querer que + subjunctive
text: When one person wants another person to do something, use querer que followed by the subjunctive: Quiero que vengas, not Quiero que vienes.

title: The personal a
text: Put a before a direct object that is a specific person or pet: Vi a Juan, Busco a mi hermana. Do not use it for things: Vi la película.

title: El agua and feminine nouns with stressed a
text: Feminine nouns that begin with a stressed a- or ha- take el in the singular to avoid two a sounds: el agua, el águila, el hambre. They are still feminine: el agua fría, mucha hambre.

title: Masculine nouns ending in -a
text: Some common nouns ending in -a are masculine: el mapa, el problema, el día, el idioma. Many of them come from Greek and end in -ma.

title: Pensar en and pensar de
text: Pensar en means to think about someone or something: Pienso en ti. Pensar de asks for an opinion: ¿Qué piensas de la película?

title: Nadie, nada and nunca
text: When nadie, nada or nunca comes after the verb, the verb needs no: No vino nadie, No sé nada. When it comes before the verb, do not add no: Nadie vino.

title: The noun gente
text: Gente is a singular, feminine collective noun: La gente es simpática, mucha gente. The plural gentes is rare and means peoples or nations.

title: Adjective agreement
text: Adjectives agree in gender and number with the noun they describe: una casa blanca, las manos sucias, mi hermana es alta. Check the noun's gender, not its ending: la mano is feminine.

title: Question marks and accents in questions
text: Spanish questions open with ¿ and close with ?. Question words take an accent: qué, cómo, dónde, cuándo, quién, cuánto. ¿Qué hora es?

title: Si clauses
text: For real possibilities use si + present and the future: Si tengo dinero, compraré un coche. For unlikely or hypothetical situations use si + imperfect subjunctive and the conditional: Si tuviera dinero, compraría un coche.

title: Por and para
text: Para expresses purpose, destination or a deadline: Estudio para aprender, Salgo para Madrid. Por expresses cause, exchange, duration or movement through: Gracias por todo, Paseamos por el parque.

title: Mucho as an adjective
text: Before a noun, mucho agrees with it: mucha agua, muchos amigos, mucha hambre. After a verb it does not change: Trabajo mucho.

title: Expressions with tener
text: Spanish uses tener where English uses to be for some states: tener hambre (to be hungry), tener frío, tener sed, tener X años (to be X years old).

title: Hay and estar
text: Use hay to say that something exists, with indefinite nouns: Hay un parque cerca. Use estar to say where a specific thing is: El parque está cerca.

title: Al and del
text: A + el becomes al, and de + el becomes del: Voy al cine, Vengo del parque. There is no contraction with la, los or las: Voy a la playa.

title: Accents on names of countries and cities
text: Many Spanish place names carry a written accent that is part of the spelling: México, Perú, Panamá, Canadá, Bogotá.

title: Present tense of ser
text: The present tense of ser: yo soy, tú eres, él or ella es, nosotros somos, vosotros sois, ellos son. The subject pronoun is usually left out: Soy estudiante.
